Exploratory Data Analysis — Olink Proteomic Data

Giulia Clas

2026-09-27

1 Introduction

This report presents an exploratory data analysis (EDA) of proteomic biomarker data from the OlinkAnalyze R package — the official open-source toolkit developed by Olink Proteomics (now part of Thermo Fisher Scientific).

The dataset (npx_data1) contains protein expression measurements in NPX (Normalized Protein eXpression) units (log2 scale) from a multi-site, longitudinal clinical study. It includes two Olink panels (Inflammation and Cardiometabolic), three timepoints (Baseline, Week 6, Week 12), and two treatment groups (Treated vs Untreated).

1.1 Load packages

library(OlinkAnalyze)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)

1.2 Load data

data(npx_data1)

2 Dataset Overview

cat("Dimensions:", nrow(npx_data1), "rows ×", ncol(npx_data1), "columns\n")
## Dimensions: 29440 rows × 17 columns
cat("Unique subjects:", length(unique(npx_data1$Subject)), "\n")
## Unique subjects: 53
cat("Unique samples:", length(unique(npx_data1$SampleID)), "\n")
## Unique samples: 158
cat("Unique proteins:", length(unique(npx_data1$Assay)), "\n")
## Unique proteins: 184
tibble(
  Feature = c("Panels", "Treatments", "Timepoints", "Sites"),
  Values  = c(
    paste(unique(npx_data1$Panel), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(na.omit(npx_data1$Treatment)), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(na.omit(npx_data1$Time)), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(na.omit(npx_data1$Site)), collapse = ", ")
  )
) %>% kable()
Feature Values
Panels Olink Cardiometabolic, Olink Inflammation
Treatments Untreated, Treated
Timepoints Baseline, Week.6, Week.12
Sites Site_D, Site_C, Site_B, Site_E, Site_A

2.1 Study design

# Subjects per Treatment × Timepoint
npx_data1 %>%
  filter(!is.na(Treatment), !is.na(Time)) %>%
  distinct(Subject, Treatment, Time) %>%
  count(Treatment, Time) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Time, values_from = n) %>%
  kable(caption = "Number of subjects per Treatment × Timepoint")

# Subjects per Site
npx_data1 %>%

3 Quality Control

3.1 QC Warning rates

Olink flags each measurement with a quality control status. “Pass” means the sample passed all internal controls; “Warning” indicates potential issues.

npx_data1 %>%
  group_by(Panel) %>%
  summarise(
    Total    = n(),
    Warnings = sum(QC_Warning == "Warning"),
    `% Warning` = round(100 * Warnings / Total, 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  kable(caption = "QC Warning rates by panel")
QC Warning rates by panel
Panel Total Warnings % Warning
Olink Cardiometabolic 14720 92 0.62
Olink Inflammation 14720 184 1.25

3.2 Sample-level QC plot

This plot shows each sample’s median NPX vs IQR across all assays. Outlier samples deviate substantially from the expected range.

olink_qc_plot(npx_data1, color_g = "QC_Warning")

3.3 Plate distributions

Comparing NPX distributions across plates helps detect potential batch effects.

ggplot(npx_data1, aes(x = PlateID, y = NPX, fill = PlateID)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~Panel, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "NPX Distribution by Plate",
       y = "NPX (log2)", x = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "none")

3.4 Limit of Detection (LOD)

LOD is the NPX threshold below which measurements are considered unreliable. MissingFreq reports the fraction of samples below LOD for each assay.

cat("LOD summary:\n")
## LOD summary:
summary(npx_data1$LOD)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
## -5.1273  0.0000  0.4288  0.9440  1.5687  6.4499
cat("\nMissing Frequency summary:\n")
## 
## Missing Frequency summary:
summary(npx_data1$MissingFreq)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
## 0.00625 0.02500 0.05625 0.05268 0.07500 0.10000
npx_data1 %>%
  distinct(Assay, Panel, MissingFreq) %>%
  arrange(desc(MissingFreq)) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  kable(caption = "Top 10 proteins with highest missing frequency")

4 NPX Distribution

4.1 By Treatment group

npx_treated <- npx_data1 %>% filter(!is.na(Treatment))
olink_dist_plot(npx_treated, color_g = "Treatment")

4.2 By Panel

ggplot(npx_data1, aes(x = NPX, fill = Panel)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "NPX Distribution by Panel",
       x = "NPX (log2)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#3498DB", "#E74C3C"))

5 Dimensionality Reduction

We apply PCA and UMAP to the full proteomics matrix to explore sample clustering. Samples are colored by different clinical variables to identify potential structure in the data.

# Use only clinical subjects (exclude plate controls)
npx_subjects <- npx_data1 %>%
  filter(!is.na(Treatment), !is.na(Time))

5.1 PCA — by Treatment

olink_pca_plot(npx_subjects, color_g = "Treatment", quiet = TRUE)[[1]]

5.2 PCA — by Timepoint

olink_pca_plot(npx_subjects, color_g = "Time", quiet = TRUE)[[1]]

5.3 PCA — by Site

olink_pca_plot(npx_subjects, color_g = "Site", quiet = TRUE)[[1]]

5.4 UMAP — by Treatment

UMAP is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method that can reveal clusters that PCA might miss.

olink_umap_plot(npx_subjects, color_g = "Treatment", quiet = TRUE)[[1]]

6 Statistical Testing

We compare protein levels between Treated and Untreated groups at Baseline (before treatment). At Baseline, we expect no significant differences if randomization was successful.

npx_baseline <- npx_data1 %>%
  filter(!is.na(Treatment), Time == "Baseline")

6.1 Wilcoxon rank-sum test

We use the non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney U), which does not assume normality — a conservative and appropriate choice for biomarker data.

The olink_wilcox() function automatically applies Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction for multiple testing across all proteins.

wilcox_results <- olink_wilcox(npx_baseline, variable = "Treatment")

cat("Total proteins tested:", nrow(wilcox_results), "\n")
## Total proteins tested: 184
cat("Significant (p < 0.05):",
    sum(wilcox_results$p.value < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
## Significant (p < 0.05): 15
cat("Significant after FDR correction (Adjusted p < 0.05):",
    sum(wilcox_results$Adjusted_pval < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
## Significant after FDR correction (Adjusted p < 0.05): 0

6.1.1 Top proteins by adjusted p-value

wilcox_results %>%
  arrange(Adjusted_pval) %>%
  head(15) %>%
  select(Assay, estimate, p.value, Adjusted_pval) %>%
  mutate(
    p.value = format(p.value, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE),
    Adjusted_pval = round(Adjusted_pval, 4)
  ) %>%
  kable(caption = "Top 15 proteins ranked by FDR-adjusted p-value")

6.2 Volcano plot

The volcano plot shows effect size (x-axis) vs statistical significance (y-axis, −log10 p-value) for all proteins. The dashed line indicates the p = 0.05 threshold.

olink_volcano_plot(wilcox_results, x_lab = "Treatment")

Interpretation: No proteins survive FDR correction at Baseline, which is the expected result — it confirms that the randomization was successful and there are no systematic pre-treatment differences between groups.

7 Summary

Metric Value
Total proteins 184
Subjects 53
Panels Olink Cardiometabolic, Olink Inflammation
QC Warning rate (Inflammation) 1.25%
Proteins with p < 0.05 at Baseline 15
Proteins significant after FDR 0

Key findings:

  1. Quality control — Overall QC Warning rate is low (< 1.3%), indicating high data quality.
  2. No batch effects — Plate distributions are comparable across plates within each panel.
  3. PCA/UMAP — No clear separation by Treatment at Baseline, consistent with proper randomization.
  4. Statistical testing — 15 proteins show nominal significance (p < 0.05) but none survive FDR correction, confirming balanced randomization.

Report generated with OlinkAnalyze 4.5.0 and R 4.4.2.
